formation.title: Maharajadhiraja of Malayapura
formation.text:
Adityawarman had the statue carved on the Batang Hari, at Padang Roco where the river still runs wide enough for seagoing craft. The inscription cut into its base names him Maharajadhiraja, great king over kings, of Malayapura. It is a Melayu title in Sanskrit letters, written by a prince the Javanese courts raised, and every word of it is a claim on what Srivijaya once held.

Yet the kingdom taking shape around him is not on the river at all. It is up in the valleys of Tanah Datar, where the rice terraces climb the slopes below the Bukit Barisan and each nagari settles its own disputes in its own balai, answering to a council of clan elders and to no one else. A king may be honoured there. He is not obeyed there in the way kings are obeyed downriver.

The court must decide which of the two it means to be.

options.text: Downriver, where the gold goes and the great kings are named

modifiers.name: Malayapura Restored
modifiers.text: The court faces downriver. Highland gold moves along the Batang Hari to the sea under a maharaja whose title the Javanese courts have reason to acknowledge, and the old Melayu line is spoken of as unbroken.

options.text: Upriver, where the nagari govern themselves and always have

modifiers.name: Alam Minangkabau
modifiers.text: The court faces inward. The crown arbitrates where the nagari cannot agree and otherwise leaves them to themselves, while young men go out on merantau and return with what the world taught them.

advances.name: Gold of Suvarnadvipa
advances.text: Since antiquity, Sumatra has been known as Suvarnadvipa, the Island of Gold. The Minangkabau highlands of Tanah Datar contain some of the richest alluvial gold deposits in Southeast Asia, and Adityawarman founded his kingdom specifically to control this wealth. Highland miners pan the rivers and excavate hillside deposits, sending gold caravans down the Bukit Barisan slopes to coastal ports.

advances.name: Matrilineal Adat
advances.text: The Minangkabau practice the world's largest surviving matrilineal system. Property, land, and the ancestral house pass through the female line. Women own the rumah gadang, and men who marry move to their wife's household. This adat, customary law, governs inheritance, marriage, and dispute resolution through an elaborate system of clan councils and elected chiefs.

advances.name: Rumah Gadang Tradition
advances.text: The rumah gadang, literally 'big house', is the iconic Minangkabau longhouse with its dramatic upswept roof resembling buffalo horns. These communal dwellings house an extended matrilineal family, serve as ceremonial halls, and symbolize the continuity of the clan. Their carved wooden facades tell the story of each family's heritage.

advances.name: Silek Tradition
advances.text: The earliest structured pencak silat traditions originate in the Minangkabau highlands, where young men learn the art in surau alongside Quranic study and adat customs. Silek Minangkabau emphasizes fluid footwork, swift kicks, and defensive parrying. Every nagari considers its silat tradition a village heirloom, pusaka anak nagari, meant to protect those who venture out on the rantau.

advances.name: Nagari Governance
advances.text: The nagari is the fundamental unit of Minangkabau political organization, a self-governing village republic with its own council of elected elders, its own adat laws, and its own judicial procedures. Unlike centralized kingdoms, Pagarruyung's authority rests on prestige and arbitration rather than military force, with each nagari maintaining considerable autonomy.

advances.name: Highland Terraces
advances.text: The volcanic highlands of West Sumatra are sculpted into elaborate wet-rice terraces that cascade down the slopes of the Bukit Barisan. These sawah irrigated fields were among the earliest rice cultivation sites in the Malay world, feeding a growing highland population and providing the agricultural foundation for Minangkabau prosperity.

advances.name: Rajo Tigo Selo
advances.text: The Kingdom of Pagarruyung is governed by the Rajo Tigo Selo, the Three Kings Sitting Cross-Legged. Raja Alam in Pagaruyung holds executive power, Raja Adat in Buo arbitrates customary law, and Raja Ibadat in Sumpur Kudus oversees religious affairs. This triumvirate balances worldly authority, traditional custom, and spiritual guidance, each checking the others.

advances.name: Merantau Tradition
advances.text: The Minangkabau are driven by merantau, the tradition of leaving one's homeland to seek fortune, knowledge, and experience in distant lands. Young men, excluded from property inheritance under the matrilineal system, venture out to establish trading networks across the archipelago. This diaspora creates a web of Minangkabau merchant communities from Malacca to Java.

advances.name: Gold Caravan Routes
advances.text: Minangkabau gold entrepreneurs lead caravans of a hundred or more men on foot down the rugged slopes of the Bukit Barisan to the harbors on the western coast. These gold routes connect the highland mines of Tanah Datar to the maritime trade networks of the Indian Ocean, making Pagarruyung a crucial link in the global gold trade.

advances.name: Surau Education
advances.text: The surau is the heart of Minangkabau education. In this communal building, young boys and men live together, learning to recite the Quran, studying religious knowledge, mastering pencak silat, and absorbing adat traditions through oral instruction. The surau system produces not merely local scholars but international-caliber Islamic thinkers who spread across the Nusantara.

advances.name: Highland Islamization
advances.text: Islam arrives gradually in the Minangkabau highlands during the sixteenth century, transforming Adityawarman's Hindu-Buddhist kingdom into an Islamic sultanate. The first Muslim ruler, known in tradition as Sultan Alif, marks the beginning of a remarkable accommodation between Quranic law and matrilineal custom that would define Minangkabau identity for centuries.

advances.name: Minangkabau Bladesmithing
advances.text: Minangkabau smiths are expert metalworkers, forging the keris, klewang, and other bladed weapons for both local warriors and export to neighboring states. The hulubalang, military officers and royal bodyguards, carry these finely crafted weapons as symbols of their rank. Arms production supplies not only Pagarruyung's defenders but also the markets of Aceh.

advances.name: Pepper Trade
advances.text: The western slopes of the Minangkabau highlands produce large quantities of black pepper, a commodity that draws foreign merchants to Sumatra's ports. Pepper joins gold as a pillar of the kingdom's export economy, with Minangkabau traders controlling the supply chain from highland plantations to coastal warehouses.

advances.name: Adat Basandi Syarak
advances.text: The Minangkabau achieve a remarkable synthesis: 'Adat basandi syarak, syarak basandi Kitabullah', Custom is based on Islamic Law, Islamic Law is based on the Quran. This philosophical framework reconciles matrilineal inheritance with Islamic jurisprudence, creating a unique legal system where high inheritance passes through women and low inheritance follows Quranic rules.

event.title: Adat Basandi Syarak
event.text:
The Minangkabau highlands face a question that has simmered for generations: how shall the ancient matrilineal adat coexist with the demands of Islamic law? The formula has been spoken for decades, 'Adat basandi syarak, syarak basandi Kitabullah', but now our scholars and chiefs must give it practical meaning.

The Rajo Tigo Selo and the Basa Ampek Balai have debated the matter. Property and lineage shall continue through the mother's line as 'high inheritance,' while a father's personal earnings may pass to his children as 'low inheritance' under Quranic rules. But the balance between these two authorities remains contested.

Shall we emphasize the harmonious synthesis, letting syarak and adat strengthen each other? Or shall we declare that the adat, tested by centuries of practice, holds primacy in our governance?

options.text: Syarak and Adat shall be one garment

modifiers.name: Harmony of Syarak and Adat
modifiers.text: The formal reconciliation of Islamic jurisprudence with matrilineal customary law creates a stable and tolerant society.

options.text: The Adat is the foundation upon which all else rests

modifiers.name: Primacy of the Adat
modifiers.text: Matrilineal custom is upheld as the supreme source of law, providing stability and legitimacy rooted in ancient tradition.

advances.name: Minangkabau Diaspora
advances.text: Minangkabau rantau communities now stretch across the entire Malay world. From Malacca to Negeri Sembilan, from Java to Borneo, migrant networks of traders, scholars, and artisans maintain strong ties to their highland homeland while dominating local commerce wherever they settle. Their reputation for shrewd dealing and mutual support makes them formidable economic competitors.

advances.name: Cassia Cultivation
advances.text: The highland forests of West Sumatra yield cassia bark, a close relative of cinnamon, prized across Asia and Europe as a spice and preservative. Minangkabau farmers cultivate cassia alongside pepper, diversifying the export economy beyond gold and creating a new source of wealth from the volcanic soil.

advances.name: Fortified Nagari
advances.text: As external threats grow, from Acehnese expansion, Javanese rivalry, and eventually European encroachment, Minangkabau villages fortify themselves. The nagari, already self-governing, now build earthen ramparts, bamboo palisades, and stone walls. The terrain of the Bukit Barisan highlands serves as natural fortification, making each fortified nagari a formidable defensive position.

advances.name: Bukit Barisan Mastery
advances.text: The Bukit Barisan mountain range, Sumatra's volcanic spine, is the Minangkabau homeland. Generations of highland living have produced warriors who know every pass, every ravine, and every ambush point. Invading armies face a nightmare of narrow defiles, tropical downpours, and defenders who melt into terrain they have known since birth.

advances.name: Expanding Rantau Networks
advances.text: The merantau tradition evolves from individual adventure to organized commercial expansion. Minangkabau trading settlements along the Strait of Malacca and across the archipelago form networks of mutual support, shared intelligence, and collective bargaining. The rantau becomes not just a rite of passage but the foundation of a mercantile empire without borders.

advances.name: Basa Ampek Balai
advances.text: The Basa Ampek Balai, Council of Four Powers, represents the highest judicial and deliberative body below the Rajo Tigo Selo. These four great ministers adjudicate disputes that individual nagari cannot resolve, coordinate policy across the highland valleys, and maintain the constitutional fabric of a remarkably decentralized kingdom.

advances.name: Matrilineal Succession
advances.text: While kingdoms across the region tear themselves apart in succession crises, the Minangkabau matrilineal system provides remarkable stability. Titles and property descend through the mother's line, eliminating the fratricidal competition that plagues patrilineal kingdoms. When a ruler dies, the next in line is already determined by lineage and clan consensus.

advances.name: Highland Coffee
advances.text: The volcanic soils and cool elevation of the Minangkabau highlands prove ideal for coffee cultivation. As the global appetite for coffee grows, highland farmers add this cash crop to their diversified agricultural economy, joining pepper, cassia, and gambier as a major export commodity.

advances.name: Silat Mastery
advances.text: Over centuries, Minangkabau silat evolves from village martial tradition into a sophisticated combat system. Masters develop distinctive styles, the flowing movements of silek harimau mimicking the tiger, the explosive techniques of silek tuo drawing on ancestral wisdom. These masters train the next generation of warriors who carry the art across the rantau.

advances.name: Minangkabau Scholarly Tradition
advances.text: The surau education system produces scholars of international caliber. Minangkabau ulama travel to Mecca, Cairo, and the great madrasas of the Islamic world, returning with knowledge that they disseminate through an expanding network of religious schools. These scholars write influential texts in Arabic and Malay, earning Pagarruyung a reputation as a center of Islamic learning.

advances.name: Gambier Production
advances.text: Gambier, an extract from the leaves of Uncaria gambir used in tanning, dyeing, and as a betel accompaniment, becomes a major Minangkabau export crop alongside tobacco. The highlands' abundant rainfall and rich volcanic soil support intensive cultivation, with the product shipped from coastal ports to markets across Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Istano Basa Pagaruyung
advances.text: The Istano Basa, the Great Palace of Pagaruyung, stands as the supreme symbol of Minangkabau sovereignty. Built in the traditional rumah gadang style but on a magnificent scale, its multiple soaring roof peaks represent the authority of the Rajo Tigo Selo. The palace is not merely a royal residence but the spiritual and political heart of the entire Minangkabau world.

event.title: Istano Basa Pagaruyung
event.text:
The great palace of Pagaruyung rises above the highland valley like a vision from the age of Adityawarman himself. Its roof, a magnificent cascade of buffalo-horn peaks, can be seen from across Tanah Datar, a statement of sovereignty visible to all.

The Istano Basa is built in the rumah gadang tradition but on a scale that dwarfs any clan house. Its three main sections house the courts of the Rajo Tigo Selo. The carved and painted facades depict the history and mythology of the Minangkabau people, the journey from Pariangan Padang Panjang, the legend of the victorious water buffalo that gave the people their name.

Within these walls, the business of the kingdom is conducted: adat disputes are arbitrated, foreign ambassadors are received, and the elaborate ceremonies of the Minangkabau court unfold. The Istano Basa is not merely a building: it is the heart of a civilization.

options.text: The pride of all Alam Minangkabau

advances.name: Rantau Mercantile Empire
advances.text: The Minangkabau diaspora has evolved into a borderless mercantile empire. Rantau communities in every major port city of the archipelago coordinate trade, share market intelligence, and provide credit networks that rival European colonial companies. Minangkabau merchants dominate regional commerce through collective organization rather than military force.

advances.name: Padri Reform Movement
advances.text: Returning pilgrims from Mecca bring Wahhabi-inspired reform ideology to the Minangkabau highlands. The Padri movement demands strict Islamic law to replace the syncretic accommodation of adat and syarak. Led by charismatic figures like Tuanku Nan Renceh, the reformers challenge the traditional authority of the adat chiefs and the Rajo Tigo Selo itself, plunging the kingdom into an existential crisis.

event.title: The Padri Storm
event.text:
Pilgrims returning from Mecca bring more than faith: they bring the fire of reform. Led by men like Tuanku Nan Renceh, the Padri movement demands that Minangkabau society conform to strict Islamic law. Gambling houses are burned. Cockfighting is forbidden. The traditional chiefs who tolerate these customs under the banner of adat are denounced as insufficiently devout.

The kingdom trembles. In some valleys, the Padri seize power by force. In others, adat chiefs rally their people to resist. The conflict threatens to tear apart the fabric of Minangkabau society, the very synthesis of adat and syarak that has held the highlands together for centuries.

Our response to the Padri movement will shape the character of Pagarruyung for generations. Do we embrace the reformers' discipline and zeal, or defend the ancestral customs that have sustained our people since time immemorial?

options.text: The purification of our faith shall strengthen us

modifiers.name: Padri Zeal
modifiers.text: The reformist fervor of the Padri movement inspires strict discipline and uncompromising devotion to the cause.

options.text: Our ancestors' wisdom cannot be cast aside

modifiers.name: Adat Resilience
modifiers.text: The traditional adat chiefs rally to defend their ancestral customs, fortifying both their positions and their resolve.

advances.name: Tuanku Fortresses
advances.text: The Padri leaders, each bearing the title Tuanku, build fortified strongholds across the highlands. Tuanku Imam Bonjol and Tuanku Rao construct not merely defensive positions but self-sufficient communities with mosques, markets, and agricultural land behind their walls. These fortresses serve as both military bases and centers of the reformed Islamic order.

advances.name: Negeri Sembilan
advances.text: Across the Strait of Malacca, Minangkabau migrants have established Negeri Sembilan, the Nine States, a confederation governed by matrilineal adat law transplanted from the homeland. This overseas colony maintains direct ties to Pagarruyung, with its Yang di-Pertuan Besar chosen from the Minangkabau royal family. It is the most successful example of Minangkabau cultural export.

advances.name: Highland Resistance Tradition
advances.text: The Bukit Barisan highlands have never been easily conquered. Each valley entrance becomes a chokepoint, each nagari a potential fortress. When colonial powers arrive with superior firepower, the Minangkabau turn to guerrilla tactics perfected over generations, ambush, withdrawal, resupply from hidden highland gardens, and the knowledge that the mountains themselves are their greatest ally.

advances.name: Imam Bonjol's Resistance
advances.text: Tuanku Imam Bonjol, mystic, strategist, and visionary, wages a legendary resistance against Dutch colonial forces from his highland fortress. For years, Bonjol holds the Dutch at bay through guerrilla warfare, diplomatic maneuvering, and the unshakeable loyalty of his followers. His three-year siege becomes a symbol of Minangkabau defiance against foreign domination.

event.title: The Fortress of Bonjol
event.text:
From his highland fortress, Tuanku Imam Bonjol wages a war that will become legend. For three years, Dutch colonial forces, equipped with modern artillery and disciplined European infantry, batter against the defenses of Bonjol. And for three years, the fortress holds.

Imam Bonjol is no mere warlord. A mystic, a scholar, and a brilliant strategist, he has built Bonjol into a self-sustaining community, with mosques, markets, gardens, and wells all within its walls. His fighters know every trail through the surrounding mountains. Dutch supply lines are ambushed. Reinforcements are harassed. The terrain itself fights on Bonjol's side.

Though the fortress will eventually fall, through Dutch treachery at a false negotiation rather than military defeat, the resistance of Imam Bonjol becomes an eternal symbol of Minangkabau courage. His defiance echoes through the centuries: the highlands cannot be conquered by force alone.

options.text: Let our mountains remember his name

modifiers.name: Bonjol's Defiance
modifiers.text: The legendary resistance of Imam Bonjol inspires the entire nation to stand against foreign domination, whatever the cost.

advances.name: Adat versus Padri
advances.text: The Padri Wars reveal the fundamental tension within Minangkabau society: between ancient matrilineal custom and reformist Islamic purity. This is not merely a military conflict but an intellectual one. The resolution, a renewed synthesis of adat and Islam that survives into the modern era, produces some of the most sophisticated legal and philosophical thinking in the Malay world.

advances.name: Minangkabau Renaissance
advances.text: From the crucible of the Padri Wars emerges a Minangkabau intellectual renaissance. Scholars, writers, and philosophers grapple with the relationship between tradition and modernity, Islam and custom, local identity and global engagement. This ferment produces literature, legal theory, and educational reform that will make the Minangkabau one of the most intellectually productive peoples of the archipelago.

advances.name: Modern Rantau Economy
advances.text: The merantau tradition transforms from a cultural practice into an economic strategy. Minangkabau entrepreneurs establish businesses across the Indonesian archipelago and beyond, creating supply chains, franchise-like restaurant networks, and mutual aid organizations. Their commercial acumen, honed by centuries of trading tradition, makes them among the most economically successful groups in Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Nusantara Scholars
advances.text: Minangkabau scholars occupy leading positions in Islamic education, journalism, literature, and political thought across the Nusantara. The surau tradition of rigorous learning, combined with the merantau impulse to engage with the wider world, produces intellectuals who bridge local tradition and global modernity. Their influence shapes the intellectual landscape of the entire region.

advances.name: Padang Cultural Export
advances.text: Padang cuisine, with its elaborate rendang, its fiery sambal, its rich coconut-based curries, becomes the most recognizable culinary tradition in Southeast Asia. Rantau migrants establish Padang restaurants in every city they settle, creating an informal but powerful cultural export network. Nasi Padang becomes a symbol of Minangkabau identity far beyond the highlands.

destiny.name: The Seat at Tanah Datar
destiny.text: The kingdom has a name and a seat, and the message goes out from the highland valleys to every nagari that will hear it. What follows depends on which way the court turns: downriver toward the sea and the great courts, or inward toward the villages and the world their sons build abroad. Hold the realm steady while the answer takes shape.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Word Goes Out from Tanah Datar
event.text:
Riders leave the highland valleys carrying the same sentence to every balai in the alam: there is a king at Pagaruyung, and this is his name. In some nagari the elders hear it out, agree that it is fitting, and go back to arguing about a buffalo. In others the messenger is fed, thanked and quietly ignored.

Neither reaction is defiance. The Minangkabau have always held that the king is the apex of the world and the nagari is where the world is actually run, and they see no contradiction in the two. What the court decides to do with that arrangement is the whole question of the reign.

options.text: Let the message go as far as it will carry

destiny.name: Padang Roco
destiny.text: The Amoghapasa statue stands at Padang Roco on the Batang Hari, far below the highland seat, and the inscription Adityawarman cut into its base is a claim on the whole Melayu inheritance. A claim written on a riverbank is worth what the riverbank is worth. Take Jambi and the river mouth at Muara Sabak, so that highland gold reaches seagoing craft under one flag, and let the court's standing rise with it.

conditions.text: Chose Malayapura Restored
Own Jambi, or a subject owns it
Own Muara Sabak, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The Statue on the Riverbank
event.text:
The Batang Hari runs slow and brown past Padang Roco, wide enough here that a seagoing prau can come up on the tide. The Amoghapasa stands where it was set down, and the letters cut around its base are read aloud for the assembled headmen: Maharajadhiraja, great king over kings, of Malayapura.

The headmen are impressed. They are also aware that the boats carrying highland gold downstream pass three sets of hands before they reach salt water, and that none of those hands belong to Pagaruyung. Now they do. What was cut in stone in a season of ceremony has taken a generation of war to make true.

options.text: The river is ours from the mountains to the tide

destiny.name: Maharajadhiraja
destiny.text: Palembang was the Melayu seat long before Jambi and longer before Pagaruyung, and Siak watches the Strait where every cargo out of Sumatra must pass. A king who holds the old capital and the narrows both is the successor his own inscription says he is. Take them, and have the treasury full enough that the claim is heard rather than laughed at.

conditions.text: Own Palembang, or a subject owns it
Own Siak, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Old Capital
event.text:
Palembang has been taken. The Musi delta, the site of the palace of the Srivijayan maharajas, the reach of water from which a thousand years of Malay kingship claims descent, now answers to a court in a highland valley whose roofs are shaped like buffalo horns.

The court is not sure how to be an empire. The ministers who understand the nagari have no vocabulary for a river capital of foreign merchants, and the merchants have no interest in adat. Two remedies are proposed, and they are not compatible. One party wants the court itself rebuilt: ranks, envoys, ceremonial in the Javanese manner Adityawarman knew as a boy. The other says a maharaja is whoever controls the road, and asks for the road.

options.text: Build the court in the manner that raised our founder

modifiers.name: Court of Malayapura
modifiers.text: Ranks, envoys and ceremonial in the manner of the Javanese court that raised Adityawarman. The treasury spends on protocol what it does not spend on garrisons.

options.text: Clear the portages and widen the caravan road

modifiers.name: The River Road
modifiers.text: Cleared portages, marked fords and a track down the Bukit Barisan wide enough for a caravan of a hundred carriers walking single file.

destiny.name: The Gold Road to the Sea
destiny.text: Kota Kapur on Bangka carries the oldest Srivijayan inscription and the tin islands with it. Barus on the western coast was selling camphor to Alexandria before any of this began. Hold both, with a treasury and a name to match, and the old maritime realm is standing again in Minangkabau hands. The wharves that weigh the gold are built at the ports.

conditions.text: Own Kota Kapur, or a subject owns it
Own Barus, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Gold at least 3000

event.title: Camphor, Tin and the Open Sea
event.text:
Barus in the west, whose camphor reached Alexandria when the Minangkabau were still a rumour in the hills. Kota Kapur in the east, where a stone cut with a Srivijayan curse against the disloyal has stood since before Islam came to the archipelago. Both are held, and between them lies everything the old thalassocracy ever claimed.

What to do with it divides the council. Highland men can learn the sea, though the coast will take its price in fever from people bred to cool valleys. Or the kingdom can do what it has always done best, which is to be the source: strike the gold into coin under the king's own die and let others carry it.

options.text: Teach highland men the sea and build our own hulls

modifiers.name: Highland Men at Sea
modifiers.text: Shipwrights on the coast and crews drawn from valleys that never saw salt water. The lowland ports take their price in fever, which is why the darek stayed in the hills.

options.text: Strike the coin here and let others do the sailing

modifiers.name: The King's Die
modifiers.text: Highland gold struck into coin under the royal mark, with the river polities downstream paying their share in and the diggings cheaper to open.

destiny.name: The Young Men Go Out
destiny.text: A boy leaves the surau with his letters, his silek and nothing else, and the village measures him by what he brings home. Push the custom as far as it will go: take the nearest rantau on the southern coast at Mukomuko, teach enough of the alam to read and reckon, and put Minangkabau traders into markets the crown itself has never entered.

conditions.text: Chose Alam Minangkabau
Own Mukomuko, or a subject owns it
Average country literacy at least 20
Num of markets with merchants at least 3

event.title: What They Bring Back
event.text:
The custom is old and the rule is simple. A young man who stays in his mother's house all his life is nobody. He goes out with his letters from the surau, whatever silek he has learned and no land of his own, because under adat the land is his sisters' and always was. He comes back when he has something to come back with.

This generation has gone further than any before it. There are Minangkabau in the coastal towns down to Mukomuko, in market ports where nobody had heard the name a lifetime ago, keeping accounts in two scripts and sending silver up the rivers to villages that never saw them leave.

options.text: Every son who returns brings the world back with him

destiny.name: Adat Perpatih Abroad
destiny.text: Across the water on the peninsula, Minangkabau settlers govern themselves by Adat Perpatih, their own law carried inland and planted there whole. Take root at Kajang, let one realm of the rantau take its prince from Pagaruyung and rule in our name, as the chiefs of Negeri Sembilan would ask of us, and raise the reading of the alam again. Village law travels better than village armies.

conditions.text: Own Kajang, or a subject owns it
Num subjects at least 1
Average country literacy at least 30

event.title: The Law Crosses the Water
event.text:
Inland from the peninsular coast, the settlements are governed by clan mothers, elected headmen and the same rules of inheritance that hold in Tanah Datar. Nobody conquered these valleys. Families arrived, cleared ground, sent for relatives and carried their law with them, and the law worked well enough that their neighbours adopted it.

The court is asked what it wants this to become. Some say leave it exactly as it is and let the balai settle its own disputes, because that is the arrangement that made it work. Others say the moment is here to move people in numbers, fill the towns, and turn a scattering of villages into a presence nobody can dislodge.

options.text: Leave the balai to settle their own affairs

modifiers.name: The Balai Settles It
modifiers.text: A crown that arbitrates is heard in valleys where a crown that commands is not. Distance through the hills stops being an excuse for ignoring the seat.

options.text: Move families across in numbers while the way is open

modifiers.name: A Generation on the Road
modifiers.text: Whole families crossing at once, filling the towns and returning rich to the villages. While they are moving, nobody is counting them.

effects.name: Possible Burghers in Towns and Cities

destiny.name: Alam Minangkabau
destiny.text: The alam is darek and rantau together: the highland valleys that never submitted to anyone, and every town from the Muar river to Malacca where a Minangkabau house keeps its own custom and sends money home. Hold the peninsular ports, carry the letters to every village, and put merchants in markets across the archipelago. Then the rantau house can be built anywhere the trade reaches.

conditions.text: Own Muar, or a subject owns it
Own Malacca, or a subject owns it
Average country literacy at least 40
Num of markets with merchants at least 5

event.title: Darek and Rantau, One World
event.text:
Count it honestly and the alam is no longer a highland kingdom with a few traders abroad. It is a network: the valleys, the coastal ports, the peninsular settlements, the market towns from the Muar river to Malacca, held together by clan obligation, credit, marriage and the certainty that a Minangkabau anywhere will lodge a Minangkabau from anywhere else.

What holds a thing like that together is the argument in the balai now. One side says learning, the surau in every village turning out reciters and jurists and men who can keep a ledger. The other says every nagari should be able to put its own men under arms on its own word, and answer to nobody for it.

options.text: Put a surau in every village and fill it

modifiers.name: A Surau in Every Village
modifiers.text: Boys sleeping in the village hall learn recitation, law and reckoning together, and the ones who go furthest come back to teach.

options.text: Let every nagari raise its own men on its own word

modifiers.name: The Nagari Under Arms
modifiers.text: Every village raising its own men on its own authority. They muster fast and they go home fast, and nothing of the campaign outlives it.

units.name: Pesilat
units.text: Practitioners of silek Minangkabau, the ancient martial art of the highlands. Pesilat fight with fluid footwork, explosive kicks, and keris daggers, relying on agility and initiative over heavy armor. They are trained from boyhood in the surau, learning combat alongside Quranic recitation and adat customs.

units.name: Hulubalang
units.text: The hulubalang are the military officers and bodyguards of the Minangkabau royalty. Armed with finely crafted keris, klewang swords, and shields, they serve without pay, instead earning their share through military merit and plunder. Skilled horsemen and expert bladesmen, they are the professional fighting force of Pagarruyung.

units.name: Nagari Defenders
units.text: Fortified village militia drawn from the self-governing nagari. These defenders know every trail, ravine, and ambush point in their highland territory. Behind palisades and earthen ramparts, they fight with tenacious determination, turning each nagari into a fortress that must be reduced individually by any would-be conqueror.

units.name: Silat Masters
units.text: The most accomplished practitioners of Minangkabau silat, these warriors have mastered advanced techniques: the tiger's pounce of silek harimau, the ancestral wisdom of silek tuo. Their devastating combination of speed, precision, and unpredictable movement makes them feared in close combat throughout the archipelago.

units.name: Rantau Militia
units.text: Levy militia recruited from Minangkabau diaspora communities. These rantau settlers fight to protect the trading networks that sustain them far from the highlands. Lightly armed but mobile, they patrol trade routes and garrison merchant settlements, their loyalty to the homeland undimmed by distance.

units.name: Highland Guerrillas
units.text: Mountain resistance fighters who wage guerrilla warfare from the Bukit Barisan highlands. Drawing on centuries of highland defensive tradition, they ambush invading columns in narrow defiles, vanish into jungle-covered slopes, and sustain themselves from hidden highland gardens. Their knowledge of the terrain makes conventional military operations against them extraordinarily costly.

units.name: Rantau Trader
units.text: A fast, lightly armed trading vessel designed for the Minangkabau diaspora's maritime commerce. These ships carry gold, pepper, cassia, and other highland products to markets across the archipelago, prioritizing speed and cargo capacity over firepower. The rantau trader is the maritime extension of the merantau tradition.

buildings.name: Gold Smeltery
buildings.text: A facility for processing alluvial gold from the highland rivers of Tanah Datar. Minangkabau gold workers refine raw placer gold into ingots and ornamental pieces, producing the wealth that first attracted Adityawarman to establish his kingdom in the Sumatran highlands.

children.text: Gold is produced in the market

buildings.name: Rumah Gadang
buildings.text: The iconic Minangkabau longhouse with its soaring buffalo-horn roof. This communal dwelling houses an extended matrilineal family, serves as a ceremonial hall, and stores the accumulated wealth and heritage of the clan. Its carved and painted facade tells the story of each family's ancestry.

buildings.name: Sawah Terraces
buildings.text: Elaborate wet-rice terraces carved into the volcanic highlands of West Sumatra. The sawah system channels mountain water through intricate irrigation networks to feed terraced paddies, producing rice harvests that sustain the highland population and underpin Minangkabau prosperity.

children.text: Rice is produced in the market

buildings.name: Rantau Trading Post
buildings.text: A trading outpost established by Minangkabau rantau migrants. These posts serve as hubs for the diaspora's commercial network, providing warehousing, credit, and mutual support for migrant traders far from the highlands.

buildings.name: Surau
buildings.text: The traditional Minangkabau communal learning center where young men live, pray, and study. Boys learn Quranic recitation, Islamic jurisprudence, pencak silat, and adat customs under the guidance of resident scholars. The surau has produced generations of Nusantara intellectuals.

buildings.name: Pepper Warehouse
buildings.text: A storage and processing facility for the black pepper harvested from the western Minangkabau highlands. Pepper is dried, sorted by grade, and stockpiled here before being transported to coastal ports for export to the wider world.

buildings.name: Cassia Plantation
buildings.text: A highland plantation cultivating cassia bark, Sumatra's version of cinnamon. The aromatic bark is stripped from cultivated trees, dried, and packed for export. Cassia joins pepper and gold as a pillar of the Minangkabau export economy.

children.text: Cloves is produced in the market

buildings.name: Highland Coffee Plantation
buildings.text: An Arabica coffee plantation taking advantage of the Minangkabau highlands' volcanic soil, cool temperatures, and abundant rainfall. As global demand for coffee surges, these highland plantations become a major new source of wealth for Pagarruyung.

children.text: Coffee is produced in the market

buildings.name: Gambier Gardens
buildings.text: Cultivation plots for gambier and tobacco in the highland valleys. Gambier extract is used in tanning, dyeing, and as a companion to betel chewing across Southeast Asia, while tobacco finds ready markets throughout the archipelago.

children.text: Tobacco is produced in the market

buildings.name: Tuanku Fortress
buildings.text: A fortified stronghold built by Padri leaders in the highland valleys. These fortresses combine military defensive works with self-sustaining communities, mosques, markets, wells, and agricultural plots within their walls. The most famous, Bonjol, withstood Dutch siege for three years.

buildings.name: Literary Academy
buildings.text: An intellectual center where Minangkabau scholars write, debate, and teach. The post-Padri War renaissance produces literature, legal philosophy, and educational reform that shapes thought across the Indonesian archipelago.

buildings.name: Padang Restaurant
buildings.text: A Minangkabau culinary establishment serving nasi Padang, elaborate multi-dish meals featuring rendang, sambal, and coconut-based curries. These restaurants, established by rantau migrants wherever they settle, serve as both commercial enterprises and cultural embassies for Minangkabau identity.

buildings.name: Bandar Emas
buildings.text: The gold port. Highland dust and nuggets come down the Bukit Barisan by carrier, are weighed on the king's scales, sealed under the king's mark and loaded where the water is deep enough for seagoing craft. The seal is worth more than the guard: a cargo that carries it is accepted at every port in the Strait without reweighing.
buildings.unlocked_by: The Gold Road to the Sea

buildings.name: Rumah Rantau
buildings.text: The rantau house. A clan buys a compound in a town under another king, sends its young men to live in it, and keeps its own custom inside the walls: its own cooking, its own arbitration, its own claim on every newcomer from home. The men who fill it are taken from the capital and mostly do not return, but the money does, and so does the trade that follows the name.

list.name: Rajo Tigo Selo
list.text: The Kingdom of Pagarruyung is governed by the Rajo Tigo Selo, the Three Kings Sitting Cross-Legged. Raja Alam in Pagaruyung holds executive authority, Raja Adat in Buo arbitrates customary law, and Raja Ibadat in Sumpur Kudus oversees religious affairs. Maintaining the triumvirate keeps custom and faith aligned with the throne; neglecting it lets the three courts drift apart, leaving the executive paralysed between Raja Adat's elders and Raja Ibadat's clerics.

list.name: Basa Ampek Balai
list.text: Below the Three Kings sits the Basa Ampek Balai, the Council of Four Powers: Bandaharo at Sungai Tarab, Makhudum at Sumanik, Indomo at Saruaso, and Tuan Kadhi at Padang Ganting. These four great ministers adjudicate inter-nagari disputes, coordinate highland trade, and run the everyday machinery of the kingdom. Properly funded, the council is the most effective bureaucratic instrument the highlands ever produced; underfunded, the four offices decay into rent-seeking patronage and squeeze fees from peasant villages.

list.name: Nagari Republic Council
list.text: The nagari is the fundamental unit of Minangkabau political organization, a self-governing village republic with elected penghulu, its own adat laws, and its own judicial procedures. Recognising nagari autonomy as a permanent constitutional fact pushes authority downward and out of the throne's hands. The villages return the favour with grain, manpower, and quiet loyalty so long as the throne respects their autonomy; the moment the king demands levies beyond custom, every nagari becomes a potential rebellion centre.

list.name: Lareh Koto Piliang
list.text: Minangkabau political tradition recognises two laraih, two streams of constitutional custom: the egalitarian Bodi Caniago of Datuak Parpatiah Nan Sabatang, and the aristocratic Koto Piliang of Datuak Katumanggungan. Adopting the Koto Piliang lareh codifies a hierarchy of penghulu titles in which the great clans always sit above the rest, disciplining the highland nagari and producing reliable noble levies. Left to calcify, however, the system becomes pure hereditary privilege, squeezing the merchant rantau communities and the lower villages alike.
